Counselors are generally not ethically allowed—nor is it clinically beneficial—to share every detail of a child's therapy session with parents. While parents of minors do have certain legal rights regarding healthcare, ethical guidelines prioritize the child's need for a safe, private space to build trust. If a child knows everything will be reported back to their parents, they are unlikely to open up, making therapy ineffective. 

Instead of specific details, counselors typically share general updates on treatment goals, overall progress, and strategies parents can use to support their child at home. Most importantly, counselors are ethically and legally obligated to break confidentiality and inform parents immediately if the child is in danger, such as expressing intent to harm themselves, harm someone else, or if there is suspected abuse. These specific privacy boundaries are usually discussed and agreed upon with both the parent and child during the very first session.
